questions.prompt: What is the difference between static (`libx.a`) and dynamic (`libx.so`) libraries?
options: Static code is copied into the executable at link time; dynamic code is loaded when the program runs
Static libraries are slower because they use the network
Dynamic libraries are copied into the executable; static ones are not
There is no difference, only the file name
questions.explain: A statically linked executable carries its own copy of the code it needs. A dynamically linked one needs the `.so` at run time (found via the loader's search path, e.g. `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`), but several programs can share one copy.

questions.prompt: A static library for the name `util` is a file called `libutil{{0}}`.
questions.explain: Created with `ar rcs libutil.a a.o b.o` and used with `gcc main.c -L. -lutil`.

questions.prompt: The environment variable `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` lists extra directories where the loader searches for {{0}} libraries at run time.
questions.explain: Static libraries are only needed at link time, so the loader never looks for them.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a Makefile are true?
options: A recipe line must start with a TAB character
make re-runs a recipe when one of its dependencies is newer than the target
The recipe runs once for every dependency listed
`%.o: %.c` is a pattern rule that tells make how to build any .o from the matching .c
questions.explain: A rule is `target: dependencies` followed by TAB-indented recipe lines. make compares timestamps to decide what is out of date. The recipe runs once per target, not once per dependency.
option_notes: True: that is what makes incremental builds fast.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an include guard (`#ifndef X_H` / `#define X_H` / ... / `#endif`) in a header?
questions.explain: If two headers include the same third header, the declarations would appear twice and types such as structs would be redefined. The guard makes the second inclusion empty.
options: It prevents the header from being processed twice in the same source file
It makes the header private to one file
It speeds up the linker
It hides the functions of the header
option_notes: It is about the preprocessor, not the linker.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a header file (`.h`)?
questions.explain: A header is the interface of a module: what it offers. The implementation goes in the `.c` file.
options: Declarations: prototypes, type definitions and constants
The complete code of every function
The `main` function
Compiled object code
option_notes: Definitions in a header cause 'multiple definition' errors when two files include it.
Normally main is in a .c file.

questions.prompt: Two `.c` files include a header that DEFINES (with a body) the function `int add(int a, int b)`. What happens at link time?
questions.explain: Each `.c` file compiles its own copy of the function; the linker then finds two definitions of the same symbol. Put only the prototype in the header.
options: A multiple definition error: the function exists twice
Nothing: it works
The linker picks the first one silently
A warning about unused code

questions.prompt: What does a function declared `static` in a `.c` file mean for the other files?
questions.explain: At file level `static` gives internal linkage: helper functions that are not part of a module's interface should be static.
options: It is invisible to them: it is private to that file
It runs only once
It is available to every file
It cannot be called
option_notes: That is a static local variable.
That is the default without static.
It can be called inside its own file.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of creating and using a static library in order.
questions.explain: A static library is an archive of object files; the linker copies the parts a program uses into the executable.
items: Compile the sources with gcc -c to get object files
Pack them with ar rcs libname.a a.o b.o
Compile the program with gcc main.c -L. -lname -o prog
Run ./prog (the library code is already inside it)

questions.prompt: Put the steps of building and running with a dynamic library in order.
questions.explain: The program only records that it needs `libname.so`. If the loader cannot find it, the program does not start (`ldd prog` shows 'not found').
items: Compile the library sources with gcc -fPIC -shared -o libname.so ...
Compile the program with gcc main.c -L. -lname -o prog
Tell the loader where the library is (export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=.)
Run ./prog: the loader finds libname.so at start-up

questions.prompt: Match each tool with its job.
questions.explain: Together with gcc these are the tools of the build workflow.
pairs: packs object files into a static library
the linker that joins object files and libraries
lists the shared libraries a program needs

questions.prompt: Why should library options such as `-lm` come AFTER the source files in `gcc main.c -lm -o prog`?
questions.explain: With `gcc -lm main.c` the linker meets the library before it knows which functions are needed and may drop it, causing 'undefined reference' errors.
options: The linker resolves symbols from left to right: a library is only searched for symbols that are already missing
gcc only accepts them last by syntax
It is just a convention
Otherwise the library is deleted
option_notes: The order is not a syntax rule.

questions.prompt: What does a Makefile do when you run `make prog` and `prog` is newer than all its dependencies?
questions.explain: `make` compares timestamps: a target is rebuilt only when it does not exist or when one of its dependencies is newer.
options: Nothing: the target is up to date
It rebuilds prog
It deletes prog
It reports an error
option_notes: That would happen only if a dependency changed.
Up to date is not an error.

questions.prompt: In a Makefile recipe, what are `$@` and `$<`?
questions.explain: In `%.o: %.c` with the recipe `gcc -c $< -o $@`, `$<` is the `.c` file and `$@` the `.o` file. `$^` is all the dependencies.
options: `$@` is the target and `$<` is the first dependency
`$@` is the first dependency and `$<` the target
Both are the current directory
They are shell variables
option_notes: They belong to make, not to the shell.

questions.prompt: A Makefile target that is not a file, such as `clean`, is declared with `{{0}}` so that make always runs it.
questions.explain: Without `.PHONY`, a file named `clean` would make the target 'up to date' and the recipe would never run.

questions.prompt: Which command compiles `a.c` into an object file WITHOUT linking?
questions.explain: `-c` stops after producing `a.o`. `-E` stops after the preprocessor and `-S` after generating assembly.
options: gcc -c a.c
gcc a.c -o a
gcc -E a.c
gcc -S a.c
option_notes: That stops at assembly code, not an object file.

questions.prompt: The linker reports `undefined reference to 'foo'`. What does it mean?
questions.explain: The compiler accepted the call (it saw a prototype) but the linker could not find the function's body: a missing source file, library or `-l` option.
options: Some code calls foo but no object file or library provides its definition
foo is declared twice
There is a syntax error in foo
foo has the wrong number of arguments
option_notes: Syntax errors come from the compiler.
Argument errors come from the compiler.

questions.prompt: gcc warns `implicit declaration of function 'foo'`. What is the usual cause?
questions.explain: The compiler does not know the function's type. Include the right header (for `printf`, `<stdio.h>`) or add a prototype.
options: You call foo without including its header or declaring a prototype
foo is too long
foo has no body
foo is static
option_notes: A missing body is a link error.

questions.prompt: What does `#pragma once` at the top of a header do?
options: Makes the compiler process that header only once per translation unit, like an include guard
Compiles the header into a separate object file
Makes every function in the header `static`
Tells the linker to link the header only once
questions.explain: `#pragma once` is a widely supported (not part of the C standard) alternative to the classic `#ifndef X_H` / `#define X_H` / `#endif` include guard: if the same header is included twice in one source file, the second inclusion is ignored, so types are not defined twice.

questions.prompt: `gcc main.c -o app` fails with `fatal error: util.h: No such file or directory`, and `util.h` is in the folder `include/`. Which command fixes it?
options: `gcc -Iinclude main.c -o app`
`gcc -Linclude main.c -o app`
`gcc -linclude main.c -o app`
`gcc -shared include main.c -o app`
questions.explain: `-I<dir>` adds a folder where `#include` looks for headers. `-L<dir>` adds a folder for libraries to link, and `-l<name>` links the library `lib<name>`; neither helps find a header.
option_notes: `-L` is the library search path, used at link time.
`-l` names a library to link (`libinclude`), it is not a folder.
`-shared` builds a shared library; it is not an include path.

questions.prompt: Sort these problems by the stage that reports them.
questions.explain: Knowing the stage tells you where to look: the header search path, the code's syntax, the files and libraries given to gcc, or the program's logic.

questions.prompt: A module written in C is a header (`.h`) and a source file (`.c`). Which of these belong in the **header**, the public interface of the module?
options: Prototypes of the functions that other files may call
Definitions of the types (`struct`, `enum`, `typedef`) other files need
The bodies of the functions
Declarations and bodies of helper functions that only the module uses
questions.explain: The header describes what the module offers: type definitions and function prototypes. The `.c` file holds the implementation (function bodies and private helpers, usually `static`), which other files do not need to see. This split also lets you define a new data type together with its operations.
